bridge: From P04, distinguish text from UTF-8 bytes and run a saved Python file. From L01, open two terminal windows in the same practice folder. From N03, distinguish a local link from the application conversation. 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address: this exercise connects only within your own computer.
teaching:
Think of TCP as an ordered stream of bytes, like numbered pieces of a continuous ribbon. It does not label where your application’s first message ends and its next begins. If you send hello followed by a newline, a receiver might get he and then llo plus the newline, or all of it at once. Framing is the rule for recognising a complete message. Our first rule is simple: a line ends at the newline byte and cannot exceed 100 bytes including that newline.

A socket is the OS interface a program uses for communication. For this exercise, the server waits for a connection and the client starts it. A port number chooses the listening endpoint on that computer; it is not a user identity. Python writes byte strings with a b prefix: b"hello\n" contains bytes including a final newline. A normal string can be converted with .encode("utf-8"); the receiving application needs an agreed decoding rule to turn bytes back into text.

TCP provides an ordered byte stream between endpoints. A send call does not create an application message boundary, and recv may return fewer bytes than requested. A protocol must define framing, such as a fixed length, delimiter or length prefix, and handle closure and limits.

UDP carries individual datagrams but does not supply TCP's retransmission and ordering behaviour. An application may add those features if needed. Ports distinguish transport endpoints; they do not prove the identity of a user or the safety of an application.

For a first socket exercise, use a local-only server, small bounded input and an explicit terminator. Run the server in one terminal and the client in another. If a port is already used, choose another unused local port in both files. A production protocol needs timeouts, authentication, resource limits and more robust error handling than this demonstration.

A TCP client normally starts CLOSED, actively sends SYN and enters SYN-SENT; the server listens and replies SYN-ACK. With initial sequence numbers x and y, the third message acknowledges y+1 and the server’s SYN-ACK acknowledges x+1. SYN consumes one sequence number. Closing is separate in each direction: A sends FIN, B acknowledges it, B later sends its own FIN and A acknowledges that. ACK and FIN can be combined, but are not required to be; the active closer normally waits in TIME-WAIT before CLOSED. Acknowledging received bytes is distinct from the application consuming them. The advertised receive window and the congestion window impose different limits on sending.

A socket is a program’s endpoint for communication. A TCP connection is distinguished by local IP, local port, remote IP and remote port within TCP. A TCP port and a UDP port with the same number are separate endpoints. The video’s destination-port-only UDP example assumes one local address and an unconnected socket; connected UDP and binding/reuse rules can also select by local/remote addresses. A port does not authenticate a user.

ACK means a positive acknowledgement; NAK is a negative acknowledgement in the teaching model. For a lost-ACK trace, send packet 1, deliver packet 1 once, then lose ACK 1. The sender times out and retransmits packet 1. The receiver recognises the duplicate, does not deliver it again, and sends ACK 1 again. A premature timer can produce the same retransmission even when the original acknowledgement was merely delayed. Model assumptions about corruption detection, packet lifetime and sequence-number wrap-around are part of the correctness claim. TCP numbers bytes: receiving bytes 100 through 119 contiguously leads to ACK 120, the next byte expected. This is different from the toy Go-Back-N packet-number convention. An acknowledgement from TCP does not prove the application committed a purchase or other side effect.

UDP’s checksum includes its header/data and an IP pseudo-header and can miss some corruption. It is not a cryptographic check. IPv4 permits an absent UDP checksum represented by zero; IPv6 normally requires one, with narrowly specified exceptions. UDP has no inherent congestion control, so protocols using it must supply appropriate behaviour. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP; QUIC supplies transport functions beyond UDP itself. A congested network can still drop UDP datagrams.

For the socket video, socket() creates an endpoint, not a connection. A normal TCP client calls connect(); the server binds and listens, then accept() returns a separate connected socket. Data goes through that connected socket. A TCP send can write fewer bytes than requested and recv can return a partial message or several messages combined. Define framing, such as a bounded length prefix, and loop until that frame is complete; sendall handles sending the supplied bytes but does not prove the peer processed them. Python 3 sockets exchange bytes: text.encode("utf-8") produces bytes and received_bytes.decode("utf-8") interprets them. Empty bytes from TCP recv indicate end of stream; a zero-length UDP datagram has a different meaning. Keep any practice on an explicitly local disposable fixture, add timeouts and size limits, and close sockets reliably. No external connection is required for the native paper trace.

The revised example puts time and size limits on both sides. settimeout makes a stalled operation fail instead of waiting forever. b"" is an empty byte string; data += part appends the newly received bytes. recv(100-len(data)) asks for no more than the remaining capacity, but may return fewer bytes. An empty result means TCP ended, not “try again until data appears”. sendall sends the supplied bytes or raises an error; it still does not prove that the other application completed a requested action.
example:
# server.py — run this file first in terminal 1
import socket
with socket.socket() as server:
    server.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    server.settimeout(60)  # time allowed to start the client
    server.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8765))
    server.listen(1)
    conn, address = server.accept()
    with conn:
        conn.settimeout(3)
        data = b""
        while b"\n" not in data and len(data) < 100:
            part = conn.recv(100 - len(data))
            if not part:
                break
            data += part
        reply = b"OK\n" if data == b"hello\n" else b"NO\n"
        conn.sendall(reply)

# client.py — save separately; run in terminal 2
import socket
with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8765), timeout=3) as client:
    client.sendall(b"hello\n")
    reply = b""
    while b"\n" not in reply and len(reply) < 100:
        part = client.recv(100 - len(reply))
        if not part:
            break
        reply += part
    if not reply.endswith(b"\n"):
        raise ValueError("Incomplete response line")
    print(reply)
# Expected client output: b'OK\n'; server exits after this one request.
explanation: Copy the first program into server.py and the second into a separate client.py. Their matching address/port identifies this local conversation. The server accepts one connection, reads a bounded request and sends a bounded response. The client also accumulates the response until a newline; it does not assume a single recv gives the whole message. This tiny protocol accepts only exactly hello plus newline, rejects other accumulated data, and closes after one request. It is not a reusable multi-message server. A timeout is reported as an error; this demonstration does not pretend to recover a stalled transaction. SO_REUSEADDR is set before bind so the loopback lab can usually restart while a previous connection is in TIME-WAIT. It does not authorise taking over another active listener. If bind still fails, check for a still-running copy or choose another unused local port in both files.
exercise: Save the two separate files in your practice folder. In terminal 1 run python3 server.py using the Python command for your setup; within a minute, run python3 client.py in terminal 2. If your command is python, use it for both. If the port is already occupied, choose another unused local port in both files. Record the reply. Change the client payload to b"bye\n", restart the server and run the client again. Then trace on paper the two reads b"he" and b"llo\n" and show how data grows. A split into two actual send calls does not force the network to create two recv results; the paper trace makes that case reproducible.
solution: The accepted response is OK and the changed message gives NO. Accumulated data becomes b"he", then b"hello\n". TCP can split or coalesce writes, so a single recv equality check is not a framing design.
challenge: Design a length-prefixed teaching protocol with a maximum 16-byte payload. State what happens for announced lengths 0,5,17 and a five-byte payload delivered in two reads. Compare with a UDP datagram of length 5.
challenge_solution: Explicitly choose whether zero is allowed, accept 5, reject 17 before allocation, and loop until all 5 bytes arrive or EOF/timeout occurs. A UDP receive observes datagram boundaries subject to buffer/truncation rules, but delivery/order is not guaranteed by UDP.
